title: Learning Curves and Prediction Persistence to Under-Regularization of Spectral Algorithms in Large Dimensions
summary: We study how prediction risk changes as regularization is reduced for spectral algorithms when the sample size $n$ and dimension $d$ satisfy $n\asymp d^γ$ for fixed $γ>0$. For inner-product kernels on the sphere, under a source condition with smoothness $s\geq0$ and a signal nondegeneracy condition, we characterize the conditional excess risk up to constant factors at each fixed admissible scale $λ\asymp d^{-u}$, $u>0$, and at interpolation. The resulting risk orders describe the effects of source smoothness, filter qualification, and transitions between spectral blocks. They identify when the conditional excess risk retains the minimax risk order as regularization is weakened from an optimal scale to interpolation, and when an interval before interpolation exhibits a polynomially larger risk. We also compare the kernel risk with a population sequence risk for the same spectral filter, using a deterministic regularization scale bounded below by order $n^{-1}$. Finally, for noninteger $γ$, we extend the risk characterization for kernel ridge regression to kernels on general domains under spectral scaling, hyper-contractivity, and tail diagonal concentration conditions, together with the source and signal conditions.

title: Gradient Regularized Newton Boosting Trees with Global Convergence
summary: Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) dominate tabular machine learning, with modern implementations like XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost being based on Newton boosting: a second-order descent step in the space of decision trees. Despite its empirical success, the global convergence of Newton boosting is poorly understood compared to first-order boosting. In this paper, we introduce Restricted Newton Descent, a framework for convex optimization with Newton's method on Hilbert spaces with inexact iterates, based on the concepts of cosine angle and weak gradient edge. Within this framework, we recover Newton boosting with GBDTs and classical finite-dimensional theory as special cases. We first prove that vanilla Newton boosting achieves a linear rate of convergence for smooth, strongly convex losses that satisfy a Hessian-dominance condition. To handle general convex losses with Lipschitz Hessians, we extend a recent gradient regularized Newton scheme to the restricted weak learner setting, establishing the first global $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k^2})$ convergence rate for second-order GBDTs. This scheme minimally modifies the classical algorithm by introducing an adaptive $\ell_2$-regularization term proportional to the square root of the gradient norm at each iteration. In numerical experiments, we show that this scheme converges while vanilla Newton boosting may diverge.

title: Survey-aware Machine Learning: A Guideline for Valid Population Health Inference based on Scoping Review
comments: Published at the 7th Conference on Health, Inference, and Learning (CHIL 2026), PMLR 333:198-220, 2026. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v333/oh26a.html
summary: Machine Learning (ML) models trained on complex health surveys such as the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) often ignore primary sampling units, stratification variables, and sampling weights. This practice violates the independence assumptions of standard evaluation methods. As a result, estimates become biased, uncertainty is underestimated, and fairness assessments fail to reflect population-level disparities. We propose Survey-aware Machine Learning (SaML), a nine-step guideline that incorporates survey design metadata across the ML lifecycle. Through a scoping review of 16 methodological papers, we summarize existing work on weighted model training, design-based cross-validation, and survey-adjusted performance evaluation. We also identify gaps in hyperparameter tuning and deployment. We provide task-specific guidance that clarifies which steps are required for different analytical objectives. SaML provides a checklist for valid population inference from survey data.

title: A Volume of Fluid Immersed Boundary Method for Industrial Polymer Mixing
summary: Free-surface numerical simulation of polymer mixing processes requires handling rotating solid boundaries of complex shapes as well as kinematic viscosity ratios between polymer melt and air up to $10^8$. We present a finite volume method that couples a Volume of Fluid (VOF) interface-capturing scheme with a non-conforming immersed boundary (IB) method, so that moving screws are represented on a fixed mesh without remeshing. In standard segregated VOF solvers, part of the viscous stress is treated explicitly, which can lead to instabilities and severe time-step restrictions at such viscosity ratios. To address this limitation, we integrate into the VOF-IB framework a block-coupled (BC) scheme in which the full viscous stress, including its transposed-gradient part, is treated implicitly. The method is implemented in the finite volume library OpenFOAM. On a three-dimensional injection-molding test case with a generalized Newtonian melt, segregated solvers either diverge or produce spurious air-phase velocities at the time steps allowed by the block-coupled solver, which instead yields a physical solution and reduces the computing time by a factor of about 2.7 with respect to the fastest segregated run that remains physical. On the finer grid, the IB solution agrees with the conforming-mesh solution within 2% in velocity and 0.5% in pressure drop. The BC-VOF-IB solver is then applied to single- and twin-screw extruders under fully and partially filled conditions, capturing the filling dynamics and the resulting pressure build-up along the screw, demonstrating the applicability of the method to industrial geometries. The current formulation is isothermal; its extension to non-isothermal flows, required for quantitative prediction of melt temperature and viscous heating, is the subject of ongoing work.

title: Adaptive Inference for Resource-Constrained Dynamic Pricing
comments: There is some presentation issue I need to revise significantly
summary: We study dynamic pricing over a finite selling horizon when limited resource capacity determines revenue and the observations available for inference at a prespecified price. Resource depletion can remove the target neighborhood from the feasible price set, changing the experiment generated by the pricing policy. We develop inference-aware re-solving controllers that check target-band feasibility before current covariates arrive and log the pricing mixture. Target-reserved and smooth controllers take population mean-pair geometry as a predeployment input; learned barycentric re-solving instead estimates stationary mean-consumption vectors of predeclared component kernels. On an affine binding-capacity family, an exact-input target-reserved controller assigning mass $t^{-γ}$ obtains an information clock of order $T^{1-γ}$ in probability, radius $O_p\{T^{-(1-γ)/2}\}$, and, under an exposed-face reward identity, a signed fluid-benchmark gap bounded above by $O(\log T+T^{1-γ})$. Under the exogenous affine-face condition, predeclared target support, and polynomial error spending with exponent greater than one, learned barycentric re-solving has a linear information clock in probability and an $O(\log T)$ signed-gap upper bound; centered local pricing has the same orders under slack capacity and global target optimality. An exact-input, target-compatible smooth alternative without reservation gives a linear clock in probability, an $O_p(T^{-1/2})$ deterministic-envelope radius with unconditional coverage and reporting probability tending to one, and an $O(\log^2 T)$ signed-gap upper bound. Boundary results show when physical support is lost and why a $1/t$ target branch yields only $O_p(1)$ information if it is the sole target-local source. The policy reports an interval when its prespecified support and information conditions hold and otherwise abstains.

title: A Non-Nested Quantum Search for TSP: Explicit Oracle Construction Beyond the $2^n$ Barrier
summary: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a classic NP-hard problem. Held--Karp dynamic programming~\cite{held1962dynamic, bellman1962dynamic} solves it exactly in $O(n^2 2^n)$ time. Ambainis et al.~\cite{ambainis2019quantum}\ (SODA~2019) proposed a hybrid classical-quantum dynamic programming that improved the query complexity to $O^*(1.727^n)$. However, their algorithm uses nested quantum minimum finding, which complicates coherent circuit implementation, particularly the handling of threshold updates within nested subroutines. To address this difficulty, we design a quantum divide-and-conquer framework without any recursive process. We overcome the oracle-construction bottleneck by preparing a set partition state, requiring $O(n^2)$ gates and $O(n)$ depth. Under assumed QRAM model, the structured state preparation enables polynomial-depth oracle evaluation, yielding an overall running time of $O^*(1.866^n)$ for TSP. Qiskit simulations for $n=6$ and 7, using QFT-based data loading in place of QRAM, yield empirical optimal-solution probabilities of $98.9\%$ and $100\%$, respectively, in fixed-threshold amplitude-amplification tests.

title: The Montparnasse Algorithm for RNA Design
summary: Inverse RNA Folding consists of finding a nucleotide sequence that folds into a predefined secondary structure. It is useful for synthetic biology, medicine, and nanotechnology. We propose Montparnasse, a Monte Carlo search framework based on Generalized Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation, augmented with a structural prior derived from the energy model, slow and long adaptation at level 1, a lexicographic multicriteria evaluation, a local repair of the pairs the predicted folding gets wrong, and a fleet of parallel workers coupled through a shared beam whose diversity is maintained on the faults the candidates make rather than on the candidates themselves. On the Eterna100 V1 benchmark, with both solvers folding through the same ViennaRNA 1.8.5 library under the Turner 1999 model, with 100 parallel workers and a budget of 30 minutes per puzzle, Montparnasse solves a median of 96 of the 100 puzzles against a median of 90 for DesiRNA, the previous state of the art, each figure taken over five passes. It is faster on 88 of the 90 puzzles that both solve, with a median solving time of 0.9 s against 5.6 s, and it solves 55 puzzles within the first second. The one puzzle no pass reaches is solved under the same model with a longer budget, so every Eterna100 V1 target is solved by Montparnasse.

title: Automating the Expert Eye: A System-Agnostic Deep Learning Framework for Rare Event Discovery in Imbalanced Force Spectroscopy
comments: v2: Clarified methods and threshold calibration, updated test-set reporting, and refined text. 11 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: Single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) probes biomolecular mechanics at the single-molecule level, but high-throughput acquisition of force-extension curves creates a data processing bottleneck. Identifying rare specific unbinding events among thousands of noise-dominated traces still relies largely on manual visual inspection. Here, we present a deep learning workflow for the preliminary screening of severely imbalanced SMFS datasets. Using 2D image representations of force-extension curves without system-specific physical priors, we fine-tuned a modified ResNet18 architecture trained with focal loss and evaluated it on the mechanical unfolding pathways of the Ruminococcus champanellensis XMod-Doc/Coh complex. On a held-out test set with a 1.34% target prevalence (13 positive P_2 events among 970 curves), the model achieved 92.31% recall (12 of 13 events) and 91.95% specificity (880 of 957 negative traces), automatically discarding 90.82% of the dataset and reducing manual review from 970 to 89 flagged curves. We also integrated Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to provide a qualitative visual reference of the curve regions driving each prediction. The complete Python pipeline is released as open-source software with an executable Google Colab notebook, enabling reproducible SMFS screening without dedicated local GPU hardware.

title: Random coloured digraphs defined by a Markov logic network
comments: This is a major revision, especially with respect to the exposition, of the first arxiv version
summary: A Markov Logic Network (MLN) $M$ is a probabilistic relational model used in Statistical Relational Artificial Intelligence for defining a probability distribution $P_D^M$ on the set $W_D$ of possible worlds with domain $D$ for an arbitrary finite domain $D$. An MLN consists of first-order formulas, which we call soft constraints, with associated weights which are nonnegative real numbers. The behaviour of the probability distribution, including the effect of the weights, on different domain sizes is poorly understood. We approach the problem in a systematic way by studying sequences $(P_n^M(ψ) : n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$ where $ψ$ is a first-order sentence and $P_n^M(ψ)$ is the probability that $ψ$ holds in $W_D$ where $D = [n] := \{1, \ldots, n\}$. We consider a first-order language that can express a property $P(x)$ and relation $R(x, y)$ and show that all of the following cases can be realized for an MLN $M$ such that each of its soft constraints is a boolean combination of $P(x)$, $P(y)$ and $R(x, y)$ in which both $x$ and $y$ appears:  For every first-order sentence $ψ$, $P_n^M(ψ)$ converges to 0 or 1 as $n\to\infty$. For every first-order sentence $ψ$, $P_n^M(ψ)$ converges as $n\to\infty$ but not necessarily to 0 or 1. There is a first-order sentence $ψ$ such that $P_n^M(ψ)$ does not converge as $n\to\infty$. In fact, all three cases can be realized even after fixing the soft constraints and, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, by varying their weights by less than $\varepsilon$. We also show that, given any MLN as described above, we can efficiently determine which case it belongs to by inspecting the MLN. Then we show that if the weights are scaled by $1/n$ then we end up in case~(1) no matter how the weights are chosen.

title: Drift Behavior in a Bounded-Confidence Opinion Model with Media Influence
comments: 24 pages; revised version; one new numerical experiment and associated figure; some revised discussions
summary: People's opinions can change both from their interactions with each other and from their interactions with media sources. Bounded-confidence models (BCMs) of opinion dynamics provide one framework to study such dynamics. In a BCM, the nodes of a network are agents with continuous-valued opinions, and these agents interact with each other via the edges of the network. In this paper, we extend the original Deffuant--Weisbuch (DW) BCM by incorporating influence from two media sources --- one with a positive value and one with a negative value --- to capture the effects of a polarized media landscape. We show both numerically and analytically that our extended DW model exhibits drifting behavior in which a large cluster of opinions shifts toward one of the media agents. We analyze how the drift trajectory and speed depend on the model parameters, and we identify conditions in which drift is promoted or suppressed. Our results provide insight into how competing media sources can influence collective opinion formation in social systems.

title: Gravitational Duals from Equations of State II: Large Hierarchies and False Vacua
summary: We investigate the reconstruction of holographic duals for strongly coupled quantum field theories in regimes characterized by large hierarchies and the presence of false vacua. Within the gauge/gravity duality, these features translate into non-trivial thermodynamic behaviour and exotic renormalization group flows, including skipping flows between non-adjacent fixed points. Building on previous work based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), we extend the holographic inverse problem of reconstructing the bulk scalar potential from boundary thermodynamic data into this new regime. This setting presents a variety of conceptual and numerical challenges, such as near-degenerate states, large hierarchies of energy scales, and regions of the potential that are not directly probed by the input data. We develop a set of methodological advances that overcome these obstacles, thereby improving the established PINNs-based methodology and extending it to new physical regimes of interest that were previously out of reach. Applying the developed framework, we demonstrate accurate reconstruction of scalar potentials deep into the false vacuum regime, achieving robust agreement with the physical features of the underlying thermodynamics despite significant numerical stiffness. Our results extend the bridge between holography and machine learning, and suggest that data-driven approaches can provide new insights into the structure of strongly coupled systems.

title: Towards end-to-end optimization in multimaterial 3D printing
comments: v1: initial submission to Engineering with Computers; v2: 1st revision submitted to Engineering with Computers
summary: Multimaterial 3D printing enables the fabrication of functionally graded components, but optimizing their spatial material distribution alongside structural topology remains a formidable challenge due to high-dimensional design spaces and complex constitutive modeling. Using neural network constitutive laws in topology optimization requires their tangents and design sensitivities, which current approaches obtain by automatic differentiation through the network or derivation by hand. This paper combines sparsification, which reduces a trained physics-augmented neural network to a compact, interpretable closed-form law, with symbolic differentiation, enabling an end-to-end workflow from a new continuously varying multimaterial system to its mechanical simulation and design. By extracting closed-form, composition-aware hyperelastic constitutive laws from sparsified neural networks trained on experimental data, this approach facilitates exact symbolic differentiation of the terms required by the adjoint state method implemented with FEniCSx, circumventing the bottlenecks of applying neural network constitutive models in analysis and optimization. This pipeline is deployed on soft robotic gripper applications, demonstrating continuous composition optimization for highly anisotropic contact responses, and the concurrent optimization of macroscopic topology and material distribution under non-failure stretch constraints. This study is a step toward replacing conventional constitutive modeling and laborious empirical prototyping, establishing interpretable machine-learning models as practical, robust design primitives for advanced multimaterial additive manufacturing.

title: Formal Verification of Continuous-Variable Quantum Programs
summary: Continuous-variable quantum computing (CQC) is a promising paradigm already accessible through public cloud services. Yet, unlike discrete-variable quantum computing (DQC), CQC lacks a formal program logic. Extending existing quantum Hoare logics to CQC poses fundamental challenges: continuous-variable quantum programs act on {\em infinite-dimensional} Hilbert spaces; their measurement outcomes are often {\em unbounded}, so expectation values may {\em diverge}. We overcome these challenges to give a formal semantics to a universal programming language for CQC and, to our knowledge, provide the first Hoare logic for CQC. We introduce an assertion language based on polynomials over canonical observables and establish soundness and relative completeness of the resulting logic. We also implement a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator for CQC. Our tool has successfully verified CQC algorithms from textbooks and calculated their approximation errors for physically realizable implementations, proved the correctness (i.e., equivalence) of gate decompositions for CQC hardware, and computed the resource requirements (i.e., number of photon-number states) for achieving a desired accuracy in the classical simulation of continuous-variable quantum programs.

title: A New Look at the Classical Estimation Problem
summary: Bahadur's \emph{Lectures on the Theory of Estimation} develop the classical theory of point estimation inside the geometry of Hilbert space, and they record with unusual honesty where the theory strains: the locally best unbiased estimate depends on the parameter, a two-point parameter space yields an estimate Bahadur calls absurd, the odds in binomial sampling have no unbiased estimate, and the virtues of maximum likelihood remain heuristics. We present a subset of the lectures in Bahadur's notation and, at each strain, make one small modification: for each sample point, an estimate $τ$ becomes a function on the parameter space rather than a point in it. The result is the continuum of null hypotheses that Fisher, in 1955, identified with the theory of estimation; we call this \emph{generalized estimation}, and $τ$ a generalized estimator. Bahadur's own definition of an estimate, square-integrable at every distribution in the family, already supplies the domain. The payoffs are tracked lecture by lecture: estimators that exist at boundary samples where point estimates do not; an elementary lemma showing that no pointwise criterion admits a uniformly optimal estimator, which explains why admissibility, minimaxity, Bayes averaging and unbiasedness arose; assessment by information, $Λ(τ)$, with the score attaining the Fisher information bound uniformly by a three-line argument; Cramér--Rao attainment and sufficiency recovered as equality cases of that bound; and the maximum likelihood heuristics converted into exact statements about the score. Nothing classical is overturned; the classical apparatus is explained by Fisher's characterization of estimation as a continuum of significance tests.

title: On the Maximum Number of Vertices that Belong to Every Metric Basis
comments: 20 pages, 8 figures. Parts of this paper appeared in CALDAM 2025
summary: Resolving sets of graphs have been widely studied since their introduction in the 1970's by Slater and, independently, by Harary and Melter. The minimum cardinality of a resolving set of a graph $G$ is called the metric dimension of $G$ and is denoted by $\dim(G)$. In this paper, we concentrate on the existence of vertices in a graph $G$ that belong to all metric bases of $G$, i.e. resolving sets of cardinality $\dim(G)$. Such vertices are called basis forced vertices, and we denote the number of them by $\mathrm{bf}(G)$. We show that $\mathrm{bf}(G)\le 2/3(n-\dim(G)-1)$ for any connected nontrivial graph $G$ of order $n$. In addition, we show that this bound can be attained. Furthermore, it also implies that $\mathrm{bf}(G)\le 2/5(n-1)$ holds for any nontrivial connected graph $G$. This result answers a question posed by Bagheri \emph{et al.} in 2016. Moreover, we provide a complete realization of the parameters $n$, $\dim(G)$ and $\mathrm{bf}(G) \ge 1$ within the previous bounds. We consider some extremal cases related to basis forced vertices in a graph, in particular, we give a full characterization of the graphs with $\mathrm{bf}(G) = 2$ and $\dim(G) = n-4$.

title: Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent
summary:
Gradient descent (GD) is one of the most fundamental algorithms in optimization. Yet even for smooth convex objectives, the optimal rate among predetermined nonnegative stepsize schedules has remained unresolved. Altschuler and Parrilo [Mathematical Programming, 2025] showed that their recursive silver stepsize schedule achieves an $O(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}})$ rate, where $p_{\mathrm{sil}}=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)\approx1.2716$, improving upon the classical $O(n^{-1})$ rate of constant-step GD. Although the optimality of $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ has been well supported by numerical evidence for small $n$, a matching lower bound has remained missing.
  In this paper, we prove an $Ω(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}-o(1)})$ lower bound for GD, showing that $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ is the optimal convergence exponent. Additionally, we prove an anytime lower bound that matches the exponent $2p_{\mathrm{sil}}/(1+p_{\mathrm{sil}})\approx1.1195$ of the known upper bound [Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen, COLT 2025].
  Building on the approaches of [Ma and Chen, 2026; Jung, Cho, and Yun, 2026], we select specific iterations as checkpoints at which the GD trajectory explores a new coordinate, and we couple these coordinates using a chain of local functions. Our main technical contribution is a local hard function that bends the GD trajectory between successive checkpoints, resulting in a sharpened lower bound. For each prescribed stepsize schedule, we maximize this bound over admissible checkpoint sets. A recursive analysis of this maximum then yields a lower bound matching the silver exponent for every such schedule.

title: Quasilinear multiplication in the Cayley-Dickson tower
comments: 43 pages, 7 tables. v4: Added ORCID ID and institutional metadata; rewrote abstract; changed wording of some sentences and one table in Section 5; updated disclosures in Section 7. Code: https://git.tanuki-cd.com/algebraity/fastCD
summary: Direct evaluation of the defining product of the Cayley-Dickson algebra $A_n$ of rank $N:=2^n$ requires a quadratic number of arithmetic operations. This paper gives a uniform bilinear algorithm that computes multiplication in $A_n$ using $O(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations and $O(N)$ auxiliary storage over any unital commutative ring $R$ with $2\in R^\times$, with doubling parameters that are units with square roots in a fixed finite commutative $R$-algebra admitting an $R$-linear surjection onto $R$ preserving the identity. This covers every Cayley-Dickson tower over $\mathbb{R}$ and over finite fields of odd characteristic, where the tensor rank of multiplication in $A_n$ is at most $(36n-69)2^{n-3}+10$ for $n\ge4$. To the author's knowledge, this is the first uniform subquadratic algorithm for multiplication in $A_n$. In single-core benchmarks over $\mathbb{R}$, an open-source implementation in the library fastCD is over $17$ times faster than direct multiplication at $N=1024$.

title: Improved Separations between Quantum and Classical Communication Complexity of Total Functions
summary:
We refine Gavinsky's framework (arXiv:2608.18784) for exponential separations between quantum and randomized communication complexity of total functions and obtain larger separations: polylogarithmic quantum communication versus $\tildeΩ(\sqrt n)$ randomized communication with two quantum messages, and versus $Ω(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$ with more quantum messages.
  Our main technical contribution is a general conversion from quantum versus randomized communication separations for partial functions to separations for total functions. Our construction combines the communication lookup construction of Anshu, Belovs, Ben-David, Göös, Jain, Kothari, Lee, and Santha (FOCS 2016), the fully linear PCPs of Boneh, Boyle, Corrigan-Gibbs, Gilboa, and Ishai (CRYPTO 2019), and a linear seeded extractor with a short seed based on the construction of Raz, Reingold, and Vadhan (JCSS 2002). The key idea is to use the extractor to compress the lookup table into a single cell, thereby reducing the input length.

title: Mammography Foundation Models for Opportunistic Prediction of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events
summary: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death among women, yet cardiovascular risk assessment often relies on clinical variables that may be missing, outdated, or unavailable in routine care. Screening mammography offers an opportunity for opportunistic cardiovascular risk stratification because it is routinely acquired and contains vascular features, including breast arterial calcifications (BAC), that are associated with cardiovascular risk and events. We evaluate whether mammography specific foundation models, originally pretrained for breast cancer related tasks, can transfer to cardiovascular risk prediction without cardiovascular specific supervision or explicit BAC annotation. We constructed a 5-year major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) cohort of 22,497 women linked to electronic health record outcomes, including 500 events (2.22% prevalence).Using only the screening mammogram, the foundation models achieved AUROCs of 0.823 and 0.822, recovering most of the gain of a clinical risk factor model (AUROC 0.859) over an age-only model (0.765), without requiring any clinical variables. Both foundation models evaluated assigned substantially higher predicted risk to patients with radiologist documented BAC, despite BAC never being used as a training label, and showed activation patterns consistent with vascular findings. Together, these findings suggest that mammography foundation models can recover clinically relevant cardiovascular risk information directly from mammographic pixels and suggest that screening mammography may provide an opportunistic source of cardiovascular risk information to complement conventional clinical assessment without additional imaging.

title: A translation of Maehara's "Eine Darstellung der Intuitionistischen Logik in der Klassischen"
summary: A key motivation for Heyting's intuitionistic logic was to gain a formal notion of Brouwer's idea of mathematics as a "construction of the mind". One might thus argue that Heyting's Calculus should also correspond to a notion of provability. Inspired by this idea, Gödel formalised this connection via an embedding into a modal calculus, which is now known as the modal logic S4. While in his original publication, he only proved soundness for the embedding from intuitionistic propositional logic into S4, the converse was proved fifteen years later by McKinsey and Tarski. Although, it was later discovered that Gödel also had obtained a proof of the faithfulness of his embedding in unpublished notes in 1941. Rasioa and Sikorski later extended Gödel's embedding to first-order intuitionistic logic. In 1954, Maehara independently obtained the same results using proof-theoretic methods, even extending the embedding to one from intuitionistic first-order logic into intuitionistic first-order modal logic. This document presents a faithful English translation of Maehara's 1954 paper.

title: Agnostic Smoothed Online Regression with Adversarial Responses
summary: We study smoothed online prediction with bounded adversarial responses. This widely studied framework bridges i.i.d. sampling and adversarial covariate selection through a smoothness parameter $\textsf{C}_{\textsf{cov}}$, which bounds conditional covariate densities relative to a fixed, unknown base measure. We propose Hedge-Cover, an information-theoretic algorithm that achieves sublinear regret $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\text{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}) \textsf{C}_{\textsf{cov}} T})$ for function classes with bounded pseudo-dimension. The algorithm aggregates a carefully constructed family of experts using Hedge, with a prior that links regret to the number of disagreements between a consistent selector and a target function. We bound this number by exploiting covariate smoothness. This answers an open problem posed in \cite{blanchard2025agnostic} on the minimax optimal adaptive regret of the smoothed online regression problem. We establish a matching lower bound for the class of linear predictors. The main intricacy of the lower bound lies in explicitly constructing a challenging sequential covariate distribution supported on mutually orthogonal hyperplanes. This construction may be of independent technical interest. Finally, we revisit the well-specified setting and quantify the effect of response noise. For conditionally $ν^2$-subGaussian responses, we extend the existing lower bound under realizable responses by showing that the minimax expected regret is $Ω((1\vee ν)\sqrt{(\textsf{C}_{\textsf{cov}}-1)dT})$ for a function class of VC dimension $d$. A corresponding upper bound for ERM matches this dependence on $ν$.

title: The sublevel Flood bifiltration: towards scalable 2-parameter persistent homology
summary: Multiparameter persistent homology is a rapidly developing branch of topological data analysis that improves the robustness of single-parameter persistent homology to outliers, while still capturing the metric characteristics of the data. However, a notable limitation is its lack of scalability. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for efficiently computing 2-parameter persistent homology on large point sets. Our work extends the Flood filtration, originally developed for single-parameter persistence. Our construction, called the sublevel Flood bifiltration, offers a scalable approximation of the sublevel offset bifiltration. We show that it benefits from theoretical stability properties and describe how to compute it efficiently. We demonstrate the performance of our approach in classification tasks on low-dimensional synthetic datasets, where density awareness is critical, as well as on real-world time series datasets.

title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
summary: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $ν= 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

title: Identifying codes of Archimedean grids
summary: An identifying code of a graph is a dominating set $C$ such that the sets $N[v]\cap C$ are pairwise distinct. The minimum density of an identifying code has been studied extensively for several infinite grids. It is known to be $1/4$ for the triangular grid and $7/20$ for the square grid, whereas for the hexagonal grid the problem is still open, between $5/12$ and $53/126$. These three grids are the regular members of the family of the eleven Archimedean grids. In this paper, we start a systematic study of identifying codes in this family. We determine the minimum density for five of the nine Archimedean grids for which it was not known: it is $2/3$ for the truncated hexagonal grid, $3/7$ for the truncated square grid, and $1/3$ for the trihexagonal (kagome) grid, the elongated triangular grid and the snub hexagonal grid. All lower bounds are proved by the discharging method. For the three remaining non-regular Archimedean grids, we also obtain some bounds: the minimum density lies between $3/7$ and $13/30$ for the truncated trihexagonal grid, between $1/3$ and $11/30$ for the rhombitrihexagonal grid, and between $2/7$ and $9/28$ for the snub square grid. As a by-product, we prove that every identifying code of a cubic graph with the slow growth property in which every vertex lies on exactly one triangle (resp. $4$-cycle) has density at least $2/3$ (resp. $3/7$).

title: Probing the limits of materials design via a comprehensive crystal database of 14.6 million structures with 140 properties
comments: 27 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Supplementary Information (50 pages) is provided as an ancillary file
summary: Forward screening and inverse design drive materials discovery, yet their limits remain unquantified because records of known crystal structures and properties are fragmented across databases. Consequently, forward screening leaves known crystals underexplored for new functions, whereas generative and autonomous discovery has repeatedly reported known phases or close variants as new materials. Here we match structures across 55 databases to assemble MateriaViva, a unified database of 14.6 million distinct crystals and over one billion property values. To provide the missing properties of every structure, a task we term property completion, we develop an equivariant Crystal Graph Transformer Network with state-of-the-art accuracy on nine benchmark tasks and apply 140 property-prediction models across the database. These predictions reveal the underestimated potential of forward screening, identifying tens of thousands of high-performance candidates among previously synthesized or computationally studied materials that lack recorded target-property values. Conversely, comparison with MateriaViva shows that the novelty of inverse design has been overestimated, as 55-100% of inverse-designed structures are not new. Under equal density functional theory verification budgets for bulk-modulus design, inverse design yields a higher fraction of qualifying candidates, whereas forward screening reaches the higher bulk modulus. MateriaViva thus provides a comprehensive reference for probing the limits of both paradigms, revealing unrecognized performance in known crystals and directing inverse design beyond reported structures.

title: Sensorimotor behavior from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome
comments: 44 pages: the manuscript with six figures, and the Supplementary Information (4 figures, 9 tables) appended. v2: text revised, figures re-set at a larger type size, one control of the learning rule added (Supplementary Table 9), errors of wording and reporting corrected; no conclusion has changed
summary: Connectomes map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behavior follows from the wiring is unknown. Here we turn one such connectome into a spiking network of 172,433 neurons with a published brain model's untuned parameters, and run it alone and inside a simulated body. Two fixed rules connect them: odors and looming objects set the firing of the sensory neurons, and the firing of the leg motor neurons moves the legs. Outside the body, a pathway of known function conducts when it supplies a few percent or more of its target's input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to nearly every odor source. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches far fewer, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none. Navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odor into avoidance, and the learning is associative once one class of olfactory synapse is scaled. An untrained connectome supports a behavior and its learned reversal. The pathways it cannot drive show what the wiring diagram leaves out.

title: Inductive Grounded Arithmetic: Goodstein, the Hydra, and $Γ_0$
summary: What does a recursive definition mean in a grounded logic, where a sentence is true only if a terminating process makes it so? This paper takes Kripke's answer for truth, the least fixed point, as a rule. Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) writes any recursive definition as one self-referential term; Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA) adds the elimination rule for every positive one, making each an inductive definition. IGA is omega-sound and proof-grounded: sound and complete for a semantics whose certificates are its own proofs. IGA proves Goodstein's theorem, the Kirby-Paris hydra game for primitive recursive strategies, and, along Gentzen's route, the consistency of Peano Arithmetic. IGA certifies the Veblen notation below every $\varphi(n,0)$: its accessibility ordinal there is $\varphi(ω,0)$, that of the paracomplete truth theory PKF. Every theorem is machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL; order types and PKF's ordinal are cited. IGA proves the Veblen notation well-founded exactly when it admits bivalence of accessibility for it, which it does not, and that bivalence is sound exactly when the order is well-founded. So $Γ_0$ lies exactly one instance of excluded middle away, and that instance, the well-foundedness sentence and one membership claim in an internal form of Kleene's $\mathcal{O}$ are interderivable over IGA. Bivalence at the Bachmann-Howard order keeps proof-groundedness. One such claim buys well-foundedness of the countable part of Buchholz's notation at every finite level, of type $ψ_0(Ω_ω)$, and $k$ stratified bivalence rules give a proof-grounded system proving the countable part up to level $k$ well-founded; $k$ iterated closings-off of truth do too, sound only for a closed-off model. Unrestricted conditional proof is inconsistent (Curry's paradox); the purchase is implication at a hypothesis not provably decided.

title: Converse symplectic interlacing via low-rank singular value perturbations
comments: A new section has been added. It provides an algorithm to construct the realizing matrix. The introduction has been revised to enhance the readability of the paper
summary: The symplectic interlacing theorem states that the symplectic spectrum of a $2n \times 2n$ real symmetric positive definite matrix satisfies a $2k$-step interlacing relation with the symplectic spectrum of every $2(n-k) \times 2(n-k)$ $s$-principal submatrix. We prove the converse in this paper. More precisely, given a global symplectic spectrum of size $n$ and a local symplectic spectrum of size $n-k$ satisfying the $2k$-step interlacing inequalities, we construct a $2n \times 2n$ real symmetric positive definite matrix having the prescribed global symplectic spectrum and a $2(n-k) \times 2(n-k)$ $s$-principal submatrix of it having the prescribed local symplectic spectrum. A novelty of our method is building a connection between the $s$-principal submatrix problem and low-rank singular value perturbations. We also provide an algorithm to determine a positive definite matrix that realizes the given global and local symplectic spectra. In the context of the Gaussian quantum marginal problem, our result implies that the symplectic interlacing inequalities are not merely necessary conditions on Gaussian marginals, but are also the complete spectral compatibility conditions for the global-versus-local-mode marginal problem.

title: Beyond Robustness of Magic: Quantifying Quantum State Convertibility
summary: In fault-tolerant quantum computing, magic states provide essential resources for implementing non-Clifford operations. The robustness of magic (RoM) quantifies the magic contained in a quantum state and is closely related to the cost of classical simulation. However, knowing how much magic two states contain is not sufficient to determine whether one can be converted into the other using free operations. In this work, we develop a geometric framework in which RoM is represented as half the distance to the set of free states, and extend this framework to state conversion. We introduce a directed conversion deficiency that measures how far a target state lies from the states freely reachable from a given input. This quantity vanishes exactly when free conversion is possible and, beyond being a mathematically well-defined measure, has an operational interpretation in terms of stabilizer quasiprobability. Furthermore, our framework provides lower bounds on the additional magic states required for conversion that can be strictly stronger than conventional RoM-based bounds. We demonstrate this distinction analytically by constructing a continuous family of mixed single-qubit states with identical RoM for which free conversion is possible in one direction but impossible in the reverse. Our results reveal that the usefulness of magic for quantum state conversion depends not only on its amount but also on the specific transformation being performed.

title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
comments: 33 pages, 9 figures. v2: added word "any" to title, improved a bound following comment from ZM26, added three small special cases, removed unicode from an anc file, and added a statement about deep sets. v3: no new results, but many small text edits for clarity, and also added appendix with four new figures to aid in indexation of results
summary: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
summary: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

title: Rotating Walks, Derandomized Squares, and Permutation Conjugated Walks
summary:
Using the recent strong convergence results of Bordenave and Collins (Annals of Mathematics) and Chen et al. (Annals of Mathematics), we study the average case behavior of rotating random walks of Cohen and Maor (STOC 2023) and the derandomized square construction of Rozenman and Vadhan (RANDOM 2005).
  Concretely, we prove a conjecture of Cohen et al. (ITCS 2025) regarding the average case behavior of derandomized squaring for random graphs and show that the existential bounds of Cohen and Maor for their rotating random walk construction hold with high-probability for random graphs. Using the results of O'Donnell and Wu (FOCS 2020), we can in polynomial time construct a family of graphs and rotations which almost saturate the bounds of Cohen and Maor, and meet the bounds conjectured by Cohen et al. for all vertex-transitive auxiliary graphs of fixed degree in the derandomized square.
  Finally, we study independent random permutation conjugates of deterministic regular graph adjacency matrices. We prove quantitative weak convergence to freely independent tree adjacency operators when the degrees are fixed and the girths tend to infinity. Separately, a covering argument gives deterministic spectral lower bounds for polynomials with non-negative coefficients, recovering the lower bound of Cohen et al. for rotating walks.

title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.

title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
summary: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
summary: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

title: Adaptive Filtering With Reduced Computational Complexity Using SOPOT Arithmetic
summary: Implementing finite impulse response (FIR) adaptive filters by employing the sums of signed-powers-of-two (SOPOT) arithmetic may lead to simpler hardware and consequently reduced power consumption. In this paper, one evaluates the effects of SOPOT arithmetic on the adaptive filter's recursion algorithms. The filters' coefficients and algorithms' underlying variables are fully operated using SOPOT arithmetic in the whole iterative process. More specifically, one evaluates convergence rate, numerical stability, and accuracy since using few signed-powers-of-two (SPT) terms propagates numerical errors during the adaptive cycle that may impair the algorithm behavior. The SOPOT approximations are obtained through the technique known as Matching Pursuits with Generalized Bit-Plane (MPGBP) algorithm, with notable cost-performance trade-off and low computational complexity. Results are provided for the Least-Mean-Squares (LMS), the Normalized Least-Mean-Squares (NLMS) and the Recursive-Least-Squares (RLS) algorithms, considering adaptive filters employed for system identification and change detection.

title: AE-DISC: Automorphism Ensemble Direct-Invocation Successive Cancellation for Low-Latency Decoding
summary: Emerging applications in hyper-reliable low-latency communication (HRLLC) demand channel decoders that deliver deterministic performance under stringent latency and reliability constraints. While Polar codes are well suited for this scenario due to their strong error-correction capability, conventional successive cancellation (SC) decoding exhibits inherent serial dependencies that lead to high decoding latency. This paper presents the automorphism ensemble direct-invocation successive cancellation (AE-DISC) decoder, a low-latency framework that enables the concurrent computation of the left and right decoding subtrees in the SC process, yielding substantial speed-ups. By exploiting permutation automorphisms, AE-DISC decoding further improves error-correction performance. Simulation results demonstrate that AE-DISC attains up to 1.4 dB gain over the 5G SC baseline and surpasses layered min-sum (LMS) low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoders at a frame error rate (FER) of $10^{-6}$, while maintaining fixed algorithmic complexity. Both theoretical analysis and application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) synthesis results further show up to 2 times decoding speed-up relative to fast simplified successive cancellation (FSSC).

title: Conditional-Hierarchical Open-Set Deep Learning for Robust Radio Signals Intelligence
summary: This paper proposes an open-set radio-frequency (RF) deep learning (DL) framework that jointly performs conditionally hierarchical multi-level radio signal classification and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. To exploit image-based classification models, the raw radio samples are transformed into time-frequency representations using the short time Fourier transform (STFT) to pre-process the radio signals. A lightweight novel architecture using neural network (CNN), that applies con- ditional hierarchical multi-task classification heads, is introduced, and compared to two baselines including: (1) The conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) and (2) Swin-T model with multitask classification heads, where the model accuracy and complexity perspectives are considered for the comparison. Moreover, to address open-set scenarios, we introduce the fusion of two OOD detectors each of which is fitted to a Gaussian mixture model by using the learned feature space (e.g. the feature embeddings and logits) from the multi-head classifica- tion network. The overall training process is achieved on two stages following a post-hoc design: the in-set classification neural network is trained first, then the learnable parameters are frozen in the evaluation mode to process the training dataset again to aggregate the embeddings and logits used to fit the GMMs for OOD detection. Moreover, a proof of concept using experimental setup is implemented to validate the operation of the introduced models and algorithms in practical scenarios. The simulation- based trained model is fine-tuned using experimentally measured radio signals. For the experimental setup, a USRP-B210 acting as a transmitter, and an edge Deepwave Air-T software-defined radio, which is equipped with the fine-tuned neural networks is used as a detector or receiver.

title: Distributed Fiber Monitoring on a Coherent DSP ASIC: Implementation of Longitudinal Power Monitoring
summary: Coherent DSP ASICs and transceivers to date report a rich set of optical link metrics, yet these remain cumulative over the link and provide no spatial localization. This paper presents the implementation design of fiber-longitudinal power monitoring (LPM), which recovers spatially resolved power profiles from received traffic, on a coherent DSP ASIC chip. We first identify the challenges specific to DSP implementation, and describe the enabling algorithm and architecture. We then present the key design considerations for retaining the estimation fidelity of the on-chip LPM during in-service operation. On this basis, we implement LPM on a coherent DSP, a 3-nm 800G low-power DSP ASIC housed in an OSFP pluggable module, which constitutes, to our knowledge, the first coherent DSP ASIC and transceiver to perform distributed fiber monitoring and data communication simultaneously. The on-chip LPM is experimentally validated over links of up to 1005 km using 400ZR+ and 800ZR+ traffic, with no measurable impact on Q factor or module power consumption. Multi-vendor interoperability is also demonstrated, where the on-chip LPM operates on signals transmitted by third-party transceivers. These results extend coherent DSPs from cumulative to spatially resolved monitoring, allowing pluggable transceivers, deployable from DCI to long-haul, to act not only as cost-efficient transmission elements but also as distributed monitoring points across diverse optical network infrastructure.

title: WiFo-D: Wireless Foundation Model Based on Discrete Representations
summary: Wireless foundation models have shown strong generalization capabilities across heterogeneous wireless tasks and configurations. However, most existing models rely on continuous representations, limiting ultra-low-overhead channel state information (CSI) feedback, few-shot generalization, and robustness to noise. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a wireless foundation model based on discrete representations (WiFo-D), which learns multi-granularity discrete CSI representations. It comprises a CSI encoder, multi-codebook vector quantization, and a modulation-based decoder, with the learned token maps and quantized features supporting multi-rate CSI feedback, CSI reconstruction, and diverse CSI-related downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong CSI feedback performance at an ultra-low latent compression ratio of 1/32 with 3 bits per token, reducing normalized mean square error (NMSE) by more than 4.7 dB compared with the strongest baseline. Furthermore, for frequency-domain prediction with limited training samples, WiFo-D improves generalization and noise robustness over continuous-representation-based methods. The results also demonstrate its superiority across downstream tasks, including beam prediction, wireless localization, and line-of-sight/non-line-of-sight identification.

title: 20 ghz longitudinal surface acoustic wave resonators in 100-nm x-cut lithium niobate on silicon carbide
summary: Surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators above 15~GHz require a fast acoustic mode that retains strong electromechanical coupling ($k^2$). This work reports longitudinal SAW (L-SAW) resonators designed for high $k^2$ in 100-nm X-cut lithium niobate (LN) on 4H silicon carbide (SiC), operating up to 21.7~GHz and reaching a $k^2$ of 8.1\%, a maximum Bode $Q$ of 70, and a figure of merit (FoM) of 5.7 at 20.24~GHz. In this thin-film waveguide, shrinking the wavelength ($λ$) keeps the normalized LN thickness ($h_\mathrm{LN}/λ$) large, sustaining both $k^2$ and acoustic confinement. Conversely, increasing $λ$ from 292 to 471~nm lowers $h_\mathrm{LN}/λ$ from 0.34 to 0.21 and raises the L-SAW phase velocity from 6.32 to 7.05~km/s, within 1.1\% of the 7126-m/s shear-wave velocity of 4H-SiC. As the velocity approaches this limit, more of the acoustic energy spreads into the non-piezoelectric SiC, and $k^2$ falls from its 8.1\% peak at $λ= 322$~nm to 1.7\% at $λ= 471$~nm. No L-SAW resonance is observed for $λ\geq 518$~nm ($h_\mathrm{LN}/λ\leq 0.19$), where the mode becomes leaky. Overall, the FoM stays within 5\% of its maximum for $h_\mathrm{LN}/λ$ between 0.26 to 0.31, defining a design window for L-SAW resonators in thin LN on SiC at K-band and beyond.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Deep Learning for Prediction of Radiation-Induced Xerostomia in Head and Neck Cancer
summary: To develop and evaluate an uncertainty-aware multimodal learning framework for predicting radiation-induced xerostomia in patients receiving head-and-neck cancer radiotherapy. We developed a Bidirectional Attention-enhanced Diffusion Transformer (BA-DiT) that combines self-supervised multimodal representation learning with supervised Bayesian fine-tuning. The model integrates pretreatment CT images and three-dimensional dose distributions, focusing on bilateral parotid glands while incorporating surrounding anatomical and dosimetric information. During pretraining, bidirectional cross-attention integrates anatomical and dosimetric features, while a latent Diffusion Transformer learns joint representations through diffusion-based learning, feature reconstruction, and contrastive alignment. Supervised fine-tuning employs a Bayesian classifier to predict individualized xerostomia risk and quantify predictive uncertainty, with a learnable label-transition model accounting for potential toxicity label uncertainty. BA-DiT was developed using four independent cohorts (Moffitt, Emory, MSHS, and TCIA) and evaluated against baseline and ablation models. Evaluation included predictive performance, calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision curve analysis, and patient-level case studies. In independent MSHS and Emory cohorts, BA-DiT achieved AUCs of 0.83 and 0.80, respectively, outperforming baseline models. Predictive uncertainty peaked near the decision boundary, with aleatoric uncertainty being the predominant component. Uncertainty-based selective prediction generally improved net benefit among retained patients, with greater gains at lower prediction coverage. BA-DiT enables individualized xerostomia risk prediction while providing complementary uncertainty estimates, potentially supporting informed clinical decision-making and personalized toxicity management.

title: LBW-NPS: A Local Band-Weighted Noise Power Spectrum Loss for Texture-Preserving Low-Dose CT Denoising
comments: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027. Code: https://github.com/itu-biai/lbw-nps
summary: Low-dose CT denoising should suppress noise while retaining the local texture of the reference image. Matching a pooled spectrum can overlook regional discrepancies, whereas pixel losses alone can favor overly smooth outputs. We propose a local band-weighted noise power spectrum loss (LBW-NPS) that compares spectral energies within overlapping Hann-tapered patches, without tissue-specific loss conditioning. Each valid patch contributes a weighted squared log-energy difference across three frequency bands, alongside an $L_1$ reconstruction term. We compare LBW-NPS against $L_1$-only training and five auxiliary-loss baselines using the same U-Net and three seeds on DeepLesion slices with simulated low-dose acquisitions, including patch-scale ablations and lung, soft-tissue, and bone evaluations. On 220 test slices from 31 patients, LBW-NPS reduces a local spectral gap related to the loss, on $64\times64$-pixel evaluation windows, by 31.9% relative to pooled band-weighted NPS, without a statistically significant PSNR change. This improvement is supported by lower errors relative to the reference in average NPS frequency and gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) measures not used in the loss, evaluated in homogeneous soft tissue. Local band-power matching therefore improves regional texture agreement without changing the denoising architecture.

title: An LLM-Orchestrated Agent Framework for CKM-Assisted Network Deployment Optimization
summary: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) offer reusable, site-specific radio priors to facilitate environment-aware network planning. However, deploying heterogeneous network nodes to meet diverse performance requirements in complex environments is challenging and requires executable workflows that coordinate scene preparation, candidate-site specification, CKM construction, optimization, and validation. This paper presents a large language model (LLM)-orchestrated agent framework for CKM-assisted network deployment optimization, where an LLM translates high-level requirements into modular, typed, and reproducible planning workflows. In this framework, an LLM layer interprets intent, selects modules, and populates normalized configurations; physics-grounded modules generate scene, CKM, optimization, and validation artifacts; and a deterministic guarded controller performs validation-guided refinement. A common target-candidate-CKM-optimizer interface supports the registration and composition of compatible planning modules, with CKM backends, samplers, and solvers remaining replaceable. We instantiate the proposed framework for base station (BS) deployment, intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) deployment, and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) trajectory planning. An urban-block case study demonstrates automatic scene consistency checks, bounded BS/IRS deployment refinement, and collision- and radio-feasible UAV planning.

title: UMelCodec: An Ultra-Low-Bitrate and Lightweight Mel-Domain Neural Speech Codec
summary: Ultra-low-bitrate speech coding is crucial for bandwidth-constrained communication and compact storage, but preserving intelligibility, naturalness, and fine-grained acoustic details at bitrates of only a few hundred bps remains challenging. Existing purely acoustic codecs generally operate at relatively high bitrates, whereas incorporating semantic representations can reduce the bitrate, but at the cost of increased complexity. Therefore, we propose UMelCodec, a purely acoustic neural speech codec operating in the mel domain at an ultra-low bitrate of 325 bps with a lightweight architecture. UMelCodec consists of two stages. In the first mel-domain coding stage, alias-free Snake-ConvNeXt (AF-SC) encoder-decoder backbones model temporal and harmonic structures, a factorized single-codebook vector quantizer (VQ) enables ultra-low-bitrate quantization, and a multi-scale mel-spectrogram discriminator (MSMD) improves mel-spectrogram reconstruction. In the second waveform synthesis stage, a lightweight modified discrete cosine transform (MDCT)-based neural vocoder predicts the MDCT spectrum from the reconstructed mel spectrogram and recovers the waveform through inverse MDCT. Experiments on LibriTTS dataset demonstrate that UMelCodec outperforms strong baselines across most objective reconstruction metrics while maintaining competitive subjective naturalness. In terms of model complexity and inference efficiency, UMelCodec has only 19.67 M parameters, requires 1.93 G MACs, and supports real-time inference on both GPU and CPU platforms.

title: A closed-loop agentic research environment for MRI development within Siemens IDEA platform
summary: Motivation: Testing new ideas in MRI can require substantial effort to learn sequence programming and reconstruction tools and to debug implementations before the scientific question can be addressed. Goals: Reduce the implementation and debugging burden of testing MRI ideas while retaining researcher control of scientific decisions. Approach: We developed an environment where LLM agents develop sequences in the native Siemens IDEA platform, evaluate them through Bloch simulation and reconstruction, and further iteratively refine them using scanner feedback. Results: As test cases, the agentic environment was used to implement and validate a GIRF-based gradient-calibration sequence and reconstruction in approximately 4 hours, and to develop and optimize a rapid 3-second multichannel calibration scan in approximately 12 hours of researcher-guided iteration.

title: Signed Powers-of-Two Greedy Vector Approximation of Zadoff-Chu Sequences
summary: This paper explores the use of sums of signed powers-of-two (SOPOT) for a representation suitable for multiplierless applications of ZC sequences, where multiplications are reduced to a prescribed number of shift-and-add operations. The SOPOT representation is achieved using a greedy algorithm that outperforms other approaches for multiplierless approximations, such as CORDIC and CSD. The proposed algorithm is based on the matching pursuits using generalized bit planes (MPGBP), and the proposed modification enables robustness to hyperparameter tuning. The resulting sequences retain, to some extent, the good autocorrelation properties of ZC, as shown in a matched-filter detection simulation. This corroborates to their use in various practical applications across mainstream cellular systems and devices requiring moderate computational cost.

title: Personalized Privacy-Aware MARL Offloading in the Edge-Cloud Continuum
comments: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for presentation at IEEE CloudNet 2026
summary: Task offloading in End-Edge-Cloud computing enables resource-constrained User Devices (UDs) to execute computation-intensive applications with reduced latency and energy consumption. However, existing task offloading schemes generally overlook the heterogeneous privacy requirements of users, leading to inefficient privacy-aware offloading decisions. In this paper, we propose a personalized privacy-aware task offloading framework, where the privacy requirement of each task is quantified through a User-Centric Privacy (UCP) model that considers task sensitivity, user privacy preferences, and task urgency. The task offloading problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to jointly optimize the offloading ratio and the target computing server while minimizing the long-term system cost under latency, energy, and privacy constraints. To efficiently solve the resulting high-dimensional continuous optimization problem, we develop an Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (AWAC)-enhanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithm under the Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves lower average system cost, lower energy consumption, and higher task success rate than representative baselines under diverse privacy requirements.
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for presentation at IEEE CloudNet 2026

title: DISC: A Deterministic Instantaneous-SINR Combiner for Uplink Massive MIMO Systems
comments: Submitted to IEEE TWC on 4th November 2026. Copyright 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material, creating new works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: Future Massive MIMO (multiple-input multiple-output) systems will fit more antennas into compact arrays, making minimum mean-square-error (MMSE) combining computationally demanding. Maximum-ratio (MR) combining serves as a cheaper alternative but performs poorly in multi-user scenarios. Existing solutions to this either mimic the MMSE combiner using second-order statistics or, as in the optimal bilinear equalizer (OBE), rely on the loose use-and-then-forget (UaTF) bound. In this paper, we propose DISC, a novel receive combiner that instead maximizes a deterministic approximation of the instantaneous signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), obtained by replacing the random terms in the SINR with deterministic equivalents. This approximation becomes increasingly accurate as the number of antennas grows, and it exploits useful information discarded by the UaTF bound. The computational complexity of DISC matches that of OBE, with the low-complexity variant DISC-D being even cheaper than conventional MR combining. We further prove that the SINR achieved by DISC grows unbounded with the number of antennas, even under pilot contamination, similarly to MMSE combining. Finally, we numerically demonstrate that DISC achieves a sum spectral efficiency close to that of MMSE combining under full pilot sharing, while outperforming other combiners across signal-to-noise ratio, pilot length, and spatial correlation models.
